newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seen eyeing yen, lira bond issues.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seen eyeing yen, lira bond issues.

text.p: Mexico plans to place a yen-denominated issue and may issue a longer-term Italian lira bond, government officials and analysts said on Monday.

At a meeting in the Philippines, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz on Sunday confirmed Mexico would soon launch a yen bond, but declined to go into details. That deal is seen going ahead possibly as soon as this week.
The United Mexican States (UMS), the formal name of the Mexican government, may also issue a 20-year 500 billion lira Eurobond in the next few weeks.
"If the terms and conditions are favourable, we may think about it," said one Mexican government official, who declined to be identified, about the lira issue.
The federal government has been active placing bonds in various currencies, a move being watched by other emerging market borrowers.

"They (a yen and lira issues) would be consistent with them building yield curve benchmarks in different currencies," said Bankers Trust Research analyst Denis Parisien. In January the UMS placed a 10-year 500 billion lira issue. That followed a five-year UMS issue in the same market last November.

State-owned Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) has also been active in the lira market, in March placing a seven-year 350 billion floating-rate lira issue. Pemex also placed a two-year lira bond in April last year.
Mexico has also been busy in the yen market, where institutional buyers have warmly received the Mexican paper.
In 1996, the UMS placed three yen bonds, two at six-year terms and one at 10-years. In February this year, the UMS launched a seven-year yen issue.
Although the UMS only has about $1.4 billion in debt coming due this year, it has a number of other obligations, including covering the $1.058 billion in Aztec bonds called earlier this year.
That redemption is to be financed by medium-term debt issues this year, the government has said.
The federal government could also be looking at more buybacks of outstanding issues.
"The more they are able to issue, the more people will be looking for buybacks. First with the Bradies, then any other issues out there that are expensive," Parisien said.

The government has also been making repayments on what it owes to the International Monetary Fund for the funds it received after the peso crash, but the IMF paybacks seem less pressing, analysts said.
Pemex and the development banks, Nafinsa and Bancomext, have also been mulling yen issues, sources said. Pemex is seen going ahead in the second or third quarters.
